slides.title: The eight special features
slides.text: The list from the primacy lecture, repeated; direct effect is the fifth item and the subject of this lecture.

slides.title: Direct applicability is not direct effect
slides.text: Headed 'Common mistake!' and it is the distinction the exam most often tests. DIRECT APPLICABILITY: EU law applies in the member states without further consent — it is part of the national legal order automatically. DIRECT EFFECT: the provision lays down a fully operational right or obligation that an individual can invoke before a national court. Every directly effective provision is directly applicable, but not every directly applicable provision is directly effective — a regulation obliging member states to set up an authority applies directly yet gives no individual anything to sue on.

terms.def: A provision of EU law confers a right or obligation that individuals can invoke before national courts and authorities.

cards.q: Distinguish direct applicability from direct effect.
cards.a: Direct applicability means EU law becomes part of national law without further national consent. Direct effect means the particular provision is operational enough for an individual to invoke it in a national court. All directly effective provisions are directly applicable; the reverse is not true.

slides.title: Van Gend en Loos: the facts
slides.text: The same facts as in the primacy lecture: Dutch customs duty raised from 3 to 8 per cent on a product imported from West Germany, against the standstill clause of Article 12 of the Treaty of Rome. The question: can individuals claim rights directly under EU law and enforce them before national courts?

slides.title: Van Gend en Loos: the answer
slides.text: According to the spirit, the general scheme and the wording of the Treaty, Article 12 must be interpreted as producing DIRECT EFFECTS and creating individual rights which national courts must protect.

slides.title: The Court's first argument
slides.text: The objective of establishing a common market whose functioning directly concerns interested parties implies the Treaty is more than an agreement creating mutual obligations between states. Confirmed by the preamble, which refers not only to governments but to PEOPLES; by the establishment of institutions endowed with sovereign rights whose exercise affects member states and their citizens; and by the fact that nationals are called upon to cooperate in the Community's functioning through the European Parliament and the Economic and Social Committee.

slides.title: The second argument: the preliminary reference
slides.text: The task assigned to the Court under what is now Article 267 TFEU — securing uniform interpretation of the Treaty by national courts — confirms that the states have acknowledged that Union law has an authority which can be INVOKED BY THEIR NATIONALS before those courts. The argument is elegant: why create a procedure for national courts to ask about EU law if individuals could never rely on it there?

cards.q: How did the existence of the preliminary reference procedure support direct effect in Van Gend en Loos?
cards.a: Because Article 267 exists to secure uniform interpretation of the Treaty BY NATIONAL COURTS, the states must have acknowledged that Union law has an authority individuals can invoke before those courts — otherwise the procedure would have no purpose.

slides.title: The conclusion
slides.text: The Community is a new legal order of international law for whose benefit the states limited their sovereign rights, whose subjects comprise not only member states but also their nationals; Union law confers rights that become part of their legal heritage — and those rights arise not only where expressly granted, but also by reason of obligations the Treaty imposes in a clearly defined way on individuals, member states and institutions.

slides.title: Why Article 12 qualified
slides.text: The passage that became the test. The wording contains a CLEAR AND UNCONDITIONAL prohibition, which is a negative and not a positive obligation; it is not qualified by any reservation making implementation conditional on a national legislative measure; and the very nature of such a prohibition makes it ideally adapted to produce direct effects in the relationship between member states and their subjects. Negative obligations are the easiest case precisely because nothing needs to be done to make them operational.

slides.title: The general conditions
slides.text: Three, and they must be recited in every answer. The provision must confer an INDIVIDUAL RIGHT or obligation. Its wording must be SUFFICIENTLY CLEAR AND PRECISE. And it must be UNCONDITIONAL — without restriction or further conditions barring its immediate enforcement.

cards.q: State the general conditions for direct effect.
cards.a: The provision must confer an individual right or obligation, be sufficiently clear and precise in its wording, and be unconditional — subject to no further condition barring immediate enforcement.

slides.title: The three-step approach
slides.text: This slide is the exam schema for every direct effect question, and it should be written out in that order. STEP 1: does the provision itself meet the general conditions — clear, precise, unconditional? STEP 2: does this CATEGORY of EU law have direct effect, or are there further conditions — primary law, secondary law, and within secondary law the special regime for directives? STEP 3: can the provision have direct effect in THIS RELATIONSHIP — vertical, against the state, or horizontal, against another private party?

cards.q: Set out the three-step approach to any direct effect problem.
cards.a: 1) Does the provision meet the general conditions — clear, precise, unconditional? 2) Does this category of EU law have direct effect, or are there further conditions (especially for directives)? 3) Does it have direct effect in this relationship — vertical or horizontal?

slides.title: Direct effect of primary law
slides.text: Generally yes, provided the provision meets the conditions. Vertically that is the end of it. HORIZONTALLY it is possible if the conditions are met AND, additionally, the rule of EU law foresees rights and obligations BETWEEN INDIVIDUALS — a Treaty provision addressed only to member states will not bind a private employer.

cards.q: Can a Treaty provision have horizontal direct effect?
cards.a: Yes, if it meets the general conditions and, in addition, the rule foresees rights and obligations between individuals — as the competition rules do. A provision addressed only to member states does not.

slides.title: Two Treaty articles compared
slides.text: A deliberate contrast. Article 18 TFEU prohibits any discrimination on grounds of nationality within the scope of the Treaties — a clear, precise, unconditional prohibition, so directly effective. Article 19 TFEU, by contrast, says the Council MAY TAKE APPROPRIATE ACTION to combat discrimination on grounds of sex, race, religion, disability, age or sexual orientation, acting unanimously with Parliament's consent. That is a competence to legislate, not a prohibition — nothing an individual can invoke. Same subject-matter, opposite result, because of the wording.

cards.q: Why does Article 18 TFEU have direct effect while Article 19 TFEU does not?
cards.a: Article 18 contains a clear, precise and unconditional prohibition of nationality discrimination. Article 19 merely empowers the Council to take appropriate action — it is a legal basis for legislation, conferring no operational right on individuals.

slides.title: SABAM: horizontal direct effect in practice
slides.text: Case 127/73: as the prohibitions of Articles 101(1) and 102 TFEU tend BY THEIR VERY NATURE to produce direct effects in relations between individuals, these articles create direct rights for the individuals concerned which national courts must safeguard. The competition rules are addressed to undertakings, so their horizontal effect follows from their own subject-matter.

cards.q: Which Treaty provisions are the classic example of horizontal direct effect, and why?
cards.a: Articles 101(1) and 102 TFEU, the competition rules (SABAM, 127/73): they are addressed to undertakings, so by their very nature they produce effects in relations between individuals.

slides.title: Secondary law: three instruments
slides.text: Regulations, directives, decisions — each with its own answer.

slides.title: Regulations
slides.text: Muñoz (C-253/00): owing to their very nature and their place in the system of sources of Union law, regulations operate to CONFER RIGHTS ON INDIVIDUALS which national courts have a duty to protect. So a regulation is capable of both vertical and horizontal direct effect — subject, as always, to the particular provision meeting the general conditions.

cards.q: Can a regulation be relied on against another private party?
cards.a: Yes. Regulations by their nature confer rights on individuals which national courts must protect (Muñoz, C-253/00), so they are capable of horizontal as well as vertical direct effect — provided the specific provision is clear, precise and unconditional.

slides.title: Decisions
slides.text: Split by addressee. An ADDRESSED decision may be addressed to a member state — in which case it can produce vertical direct effect against that state — or to a private party, where it simply binds that party. A NON-ADDRESSED decision binds generally. As always the provision relied on must itself be clear, precise and unconditional.

slides.title: What could be the issue?
slides.text: The rhetorical set-up: a directive binds only as to the result and is addressed to member states, so how could an individual ever rely on it?

slides.title: The rule, and then the exceptions
slides.text: The slide states it in capitals and it should be the first sentence of any answer: THE RULE IS THAT DIRECTIVES HAVE NO DIRECT EFFECT. Everything that follows — vertical direct effect, indirect effect, incidental effect — is an exception or a workaround, and structuring the answer that way is what earns marks.

cards.q: What is the starting rule on the direct effect of directives?
cards.a: That directives have NO direct effect. Vertical direct effect and the various workarounds are exceptions to that rule and must be presented as such.

slides.title: Ratti: the facts
slides.text: Case 148/78, alongside Van Duyn (41/74). The solvent manufacturer Ratti labelled the benzene content of his products in accordance with a directive on the classification, packaging and labelling of dangerous preparations, but not in accordance with the stricter national law — which should already have been adapted to the directive, the deadline having expired. Ratti was prosecuted for breaching national law. Could he invoke the directive as a DEFENCE in criminal proceedings?

slides.title: Why vertical direct effect is allowed
slides.text: Three reasons. FUNCTIONALITY: a directive would lose its effet utile if a defaulting state could rely on its own failure. The ROLE OF THE PRELIMINARY REFERENCE, as in Van Gend en Loos. And ESTOPPEL: a member state may not profit from its own failure to implement properly. The slide sums it up — vertical direct effect is a REPAIR TOOL for implementation errors, not a general property of directives.

terms.def: A member state cannot rely on its own failure to transpose a directive as against individuals.

cards.q: On what grounds does the Court allow vertical direct effect of directives?
cards.a: Functionality (effet utile would be lost), the role of the preliminary reference, and estoppel — a state may not benefit from its own failure to implement. It is a repair tool for implementation errors.

slides.title: The three extra conditions
slides.text: Vertical direct effect of a directive requires, on top of the general conditions: an ERROR IN IMPLEMENTATION — no implementation, incorrect implementation, or correct implementation that is not correctly applied in practice; and that the TIME-LIMIT for implementation has passed. Together with the general conditions that makes five things to check, and an answer that checks all five in order cannot go far wrong.

cards.q: List everything that must be shown for the vertical direct effect of a directive.
cards.a: The provision must be clear, precise and unconditional and confer an individual right; there must be an implementation error — none, incorrect, or correct but misapplied; the transposition deadline must have expired; and the defendant must be the state or an emanation of it.

cards.q: Does a correctly transposed directive ever produce direct effect?
cards.a: Yes — where the correct transposition is not correctly APPLIED in practice. The implementation error can lie in the application, not only in the legislation.

slides.title: Before the deadline: the standstill obligation
slides.text: The period before the deadline is not empty. Member states must not frustrate the objectives of a directive in the meantime — Inter-Environnement Wallonie (C-129/96) and Schwarze Sulm (C-346/14) — and national courts must refrain from interpreting national law in a way that would seriously compromise the attainment of the directive's objectives, Adeneler (C-212/04). Compare the international law half: this is the EU counterpart of Article 18 VCLT.

terms.def: During the transposition period member states must not adopt measures liable seriously to compromise the directive's result.

cards.q: The transposition deadline of a directive has not yet expired. Does the directive have any effect?
cards.a: Yes, though not direct effect: the member state must refrain from measures liable seriously to compromise the directive's objectives (Inter-Environnement Wallonie), and courts must not interpret national law so as to prejudice them (Adeneler).

slides.title: Two limits on vertical direct effect
slides.text: NO INVERSE DIRECT EFFECT: the state cannot rely on an unimplemented directive AGAINST an individual — Kolpinghuis Nijmegen (80/86). That follows directly from the estoppel rationale. And NO CRIMINAL LIABILITY: a directive cannot of itself determine or aggravate criminal liability — Berlusconi (C-387/02 and others). Both limits protect the individual, which is the whole point of the doctrine.

terms.def: A state invoking an unimplemented directive against an individual — not permitted.

cards.q: Can a member state rely on an unimplemented directive against an individual?
cards.a: No — inverse direct effect is excluded (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen, 80/86), and a directive can never of itself create or aggravate criminal liability (Berlusconi).

slides.title: No horizontal direct effect
slides.text: Marshall I (C-152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92) and Delena Wells (C-201/02) all confirm it: the rule stays the rule. A directive cannot be invoked against another private party, however unjust that may look — the classic illustration being Marshall herself, who won because her employer happened to be a health authority, while an identically placed employee of a private company would have lost.

cards.q: Two employees are dismissed on identical discriminatory grounds under an untransposed directive; one works for a ministry, the other for a private firm. Who can rely on the directive?
cards.a: Only the ministry's employee — vertical direct effect. The private firm's employee cannot: directives have no horizontal direct effect (Marshall I, Faccini Dori). Their routes are consistent interpretation and state liability.

slides.title: Why not horizontally?
slides.text: Four reasons. A directive is ADDRESSED ONLY TO MEMBER STATES under Article 288(3) TFEU. There is no 'wrongdoing' by the individual — the estoppel argument does not reach them. Horizontal effect would ERODE THE DISTINCTION between regulations and directives. And legal certainty: a private party cannot be expected to know an unimplemented directive binds them.

cards.q: Give the reasons why directives have no horizontal direct effect.
cards.a: They are addressed only to member states (Art 288(3) TFEU); the private party has committed no wrongdoing, so estoppel does not apply; horizontal effect would blur the difference between regulations and directives; and legal certainty.

slides.title: The five workarounds
slides.text: No exceptions, says the slide, but workarounds — and this list is what separates a good answer from a mediocre one. 1) Interpreting the MEANING OF STATE broadly, so that more defendants count as emanations of the state. 2) The duty of CONSISTENT INTERPRETATION of national law with the directive — indirect effect. 3) TRIANGULAR SITUATIONS and the incidental effect of directives, where a directive relied on against the state has adverse repercussions for a third private party. 4) Directives that express GENERAL PRINCIPLES of EU law, which have their own effect (the Mangold/Kücükdeveci line). 5) Benefits of a regulation made conditional by a directive. When a case has no vertical route, work down this list.

terms.def: The duty of national courts to interpret national law as far as possible in conformity with a directive.
A directive invoked against the state whose application adversely affects a third private party — permitted as an incidental effect.

cards.q: A claimant cannot use vertical direct effect because the defendant is private. What five routes remain?
cards.a: Argue the defendant is an emanation of the state; consistent interpretation of national law (indirect effect); a triangular or incidental effect; the directive as the expression of a general principle of EU law; or a regulation's benefit made conditional by the directive. And, in the background, state liability.

The duty of national courts to interpret national law, as far as possible, in conformity with the directive — a workaround where direct effect is unavailable, and one that binds in horizontal disputes too.
